issues.legal_issue: In an eviction proceeding concerning public premises, the party required to lead evidence first depends on whether the landlord must prove affirmative grounds for eviction or other matters on which its claim depends.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on grounds including its own need for the premises and sought damages for unauthorised occupation.
The grounds relied upon required the landlord to establish facts through evidence.
In one proceeding, the eviction and damages claims were brought together.
issues.conclusion: Where the eviction grounds require the landlord to prove affirmative facts, the landlord must lead evidence first; this is especially so in a composite proceeding in which it must also prove the amount of damages claimed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, read with Rule 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Rules, 1971, require an effective opportunity to show cause and an inquiry into the issues between the parties. Although the Evidence Act does not apply, its Section 101 principle that the party asserting an affirmative issue bears the burden of proving it applies. The provisions must be read purposively, consistently with Article 14 and the requirements of fairness governing State action. The Court relied on Dwarkadas Marfatia and Sons v. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay, Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Punjab National Bank, Shambhu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda, Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, and J.K. Synthetics Ltd. v. K.P. Agrawal.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding concerning premises treated as public premises.
predicates.landlord_must_prove_affirmative_ground: The landlord relies on an eviction ground that requires it to establish affirmative facts.
predicates.landlord_claims_damages: The landlord also seeks damages that it must establish in the proceeding.
predicates.landlord_leads_evidence_first: The landlord presents its evidence before the occupant is required to present evidence.

issues.definition: When a public-premises eviction proceeding requires the landlord to prove an affirmative ground or damages, the landlord presents its evidence first.

issues.legal_issue: A person facing eviction in a statutory inquiry must have a fair opportunity to test evidence and inspect documents relied on to establish disputed facts.
material_facts: The landlord relied on evidence to support its case for eviction and damages.
The occupants disputed the landlord’s case.
The inquiry involved evidence and documents that the occupants needed an opportunity to examine and answer.
issues.conclusion: When the landlord relies on a witness to prove a fact, the occupant must have an opportunity to cross-examine that witness; when the landlord relies on a document, the occupant must be allowed to inspect it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, and Rule 5 of the Rules require a meaningful opportunity to show cause in the statutory inquiry. Although the statute does not prescribe a lengthy hearing or cross-examination, the principles of natural justice require cross-examination of witnesses whose evidence is used to establish contested facts and inspection of relied-upon documents. The Court relied on K.L. Tripathi v. State Bank of India, Lakshman Exports Limited v. Collector of Central Excise, and Bareilly Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. v. The Workmen.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding concerning premises treated as public premises.
predicates.opponent_relies_on_witness_for_disputed_: The party seeking eviction relies on a witness to prove a fact disputed by the occupant.
predicates.opponent_relies_on_document: The party seeking eviction relies on a document in the inquiry.
predicates.noticee_gets_opportunity_to_test_evidenc: The occupant receives an opportunity to cross-examine the witness or inspect the relied-upon document, as applicable.

issues.definition: In a public-premises eviction proceeding, reliance on a witness or document to establish the case requires an opportunity for the occupant to test that evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Government guidelines about eviction from public premises do not, by themselves, confer an enforceable legal right on a tenant.
material_facts: Guidelines issued by the Central Government distinguished between certain categories of tenants.
The guidelines were not controlled by statutory provisions.
The landlord had itself referred to the guidelines, but the Court did not need to determine their ultimate effect on the applications.
issues.conclusion: The guidelines are advisory in character and do not confer a legal right on a tenant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the guidelines as non-statutory and advisory, relying on Narendra Kumar Maheshwari v. Union of India, Maharao Sahib Shri Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, J.R. Raghupathy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Uttam Parkash Bansal v. LIC of India, and Punjab National Bank v. M/s. The Lord Krishna Paper Industries. The Court did not finally determine the guidelines’ effect on the applications.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding concerning premises treated as public premises.
predicates.eviction_guidelines_are_nonstatutory: The guidelines relied on in the eviction dispute are not made binding by statute.
predicates.guidelines_create_no_enforceable_tenant_: The guidelines do not, by themselves, give the tenant an enforceable legal right.

issues.definition: In a public-premises eviction proceeding, non-statutory eviction guidelines do not themselves create an enforceable tenant right.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may waive an objection to the occupant leading evidence first through its conduct in the statutory proceeding.
material_facts: In one proceeding, the landlord filed affidavits of its witnesses.
The landlord repeatedly sought adjournments when those witnesses were to be cross-examined.
After the occupant had already shown cause, the landlord later sought an order requiring the occupant to lead evidence first.
issues.conclusion: Even if the statutory procedure would otherwise require the occupant to lead evidence first, that requirement may be waived; in the circumstances, the landlord’s conduct did not justify requiring the occupant to begin.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that an assumed requirement that the noticee lead evidence first may be waived. The statutory inquiry remains subject to natural justice and must be conducted fairly under Sections 4 and 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, read with Rule 5 of the Rules.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_proceeding and landlord_files_witness_evidence and landlord_repeatedly_delays_cross_examination and landlord_later_demands_noticee_lead

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding concerning premises treated as public premises.
predicates.landlord_files_witness_evidence: The landlord files evidence from its witnesses in the proceeding.
predicates.landlord_repeatedly_delays_cross_examina: The landlord repeatedly delays the opportunity to cross-examine its witnesses.
predicates.landlord_later_demands_noticee_lead: The landlord later asks that the occupant be required to present evidence first.
predicates.landlord_waived_demand_for_noticee_to_le: The landlord cannot insist, on the basis of the otherwise applicable sequence, that the occupant present evidence first.

issues.definition: When the landlord files witness evidence, repeatedly delays its cross-examination, and later demands that the occupant begin, the landlord has waived that demand.
